editorialPolicy.storyFidelity: Each level preserves the complete event sequence, motivations, consequence, and chapter ending.
editorialPolicy.foundation: Concrete 6–11 word sentences, one main action per line, minimal subordinate clauses.
editorialPolicy.core: Connected 10–18 word sentences with cause, contrast, and reaction.
editorialPolicy.studio: Literary but speakable sentences that preserve narrator wit, suspense, and moral tension.
editorialPolicy.safety: Historic slapstick and peril are described without adding graphic detail. Harmful actions retain their consequences and are not presented as desirable.
editorialPolicy.narration: Dialogue is acted with restraint inside one continuous chapter-level performance; no independent sentence generations.

narration.direction: Begin as a playful fireside storyteller, build quiet suspense around the first voice, let the wood sound tiny and mischievous, and end with comic disbelief.
narration.productionRule: Generate one continuous master per level and derive sentence timestamps from that same master.

livingStorybook.artBrief: A wide cross-section of Mastro Cherry's old workshop: workbench and ordinary log at center, hatchet and wood plane nearby, closet and street door at the edges, curls of wood shavings on the floor. The six beats must be readable through camera pans from log to tools to the carpenter's shocked reaction.

lines.text: Long ago, there was a simple piece of wood.
It arrived at Mastro Cherry's carpenter shop.
He wanted to make a table leg.
He lifted his hatchet over the wood.
A tiny voice begged him to stop.
Mastro Cherry searched, but found nobody.
The wood cried when he struck it.
Then it giggled, and the carpenter fell down.

lines.text: This story begins with an ordinary block of winter firewood.
One day, it appeared in the workshop of Mastro Cherry.
The carpenter happily decided to turn it into a table leg.
As he raised his hatchet, a tiny voice begged for care.
He searched under the bench and inside the closet, but found no one.
Certain that he had imagined the voice, he struck the wood.
The unseen speaker cried out, and Mastro Cherry froze in fear.
He knocked the log against the floor and walls, yet it stayed silent.
When he used a plane, the wood complained that it tickled.
The terrified carpenter collapsed, his red nose turning purple.

lines.text: Although readers may expect a king, the tale opens with a common block of firewood.
Somehow, the unremarkable log found its way into the workshop of Mastro Cherry, an old carpenter with a round red nose.
Delighted by its sturdy shape, he decided that it had arrived just in time to become a table leg.
Yet, as he lifted his hatchet, a faint voice pleaded with him not to strike so hard.
Astonished, he searched beneath the bench, inside the closet, and among the shavings, but discovered no one.
Embarrassed by his fear, he blamed his imagination and delivered a solemn blow.
The distant voice cried in pain, leaving the carpenter speechless and trembling.
Determined to expose the trick, he knocked the log against the floor, walls, and ceiling, but heard nothing.
When his plane slid across the wood, the hidden voice giggled that its stomach was being tickled.
At that impossible complaint, poor Mastro Cherry collapsed as though he had been struck.
